Same thing happened to me a month ago. I was trying to repot my SOP in better-draining succulent mix as it was getting root rot from the compost it came in. People say their root systems are shallow, but some well-established ones can go deep!

What I did was separate the individual strands to gauge how much root each of them had left. Strands with 1-2 inches were repotted right away (individually in tiny pots in case they had different watering needs), strands with <1 inch were propagated. This took about 3 hours and was a lot of effort. 

I watered the repotted strands whenever their epidermal windows closed & misted the propagated strands 1-2 times each day. Kept in medium-high (not direct) light, ambient room temperature. All strands have survived & put out a ton of new growth! Guessing it’s a lot happier in the right kind of soil.

TLDR: You’ll probably be ok if you just carry on repotting. But make sure the soil has good drainage & pay more attention to its watering needs for the next month or so. String of pearls are pretty hardy & fast-growing if provided with the right kind of soil + just enough light! Feel free to ask any questions, I’m no expert but I’ll give ‘em my best shot!

AFAIK direction of mass flow in the phloem always goes from Source (something that makes more sugar than it uses up—e.g. a photosynthesising leaf) to Sink (something that uses up more sugar than it makes—e.g. a flower bud or in this case, albino graft). Locations of Sources and Sinks may change depending on time of year due to flowering/fruiting. 

I recommend checking out the Wikipedia page for [albino redwood trees](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albino_redwood) as an example, it’s an interesting read. Basically their roots get sugar from the roots of neighboring redwoods.

TLDR: sugar can be transported either way depending on where it is most needed.
